summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for describing how MPLS routers classify packets into forwarding equivalence classes and map each class to a next-hop label forwarding entry. It lets operators configure and monitor those mappings with standard management tools.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of sorting letters into piles by destination, then deciding which truck each pile goes on. This document gives managers a standard way to see and set those pile-to-truck rules.

subtitle: The SNMP tables that tell an MPLS edge router which packets get which label path.

tldr.problem: An MPLS router at the edge of the network has to decide which incoming packets are assigned to which label switched path or tunnel, and operators need a standard way to configure and monitor those decisions.
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS-FTN-STD-MIB module defines three tables: one of matching rules and actions, one that applies the rules to interfaces in a linked-list order, and one of per-interface counters.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use SNMP to set up and watch FEC-to-NHLFE mappings in a standard way. Writing to these tables can misdirect traffic, so the RFC recommends SNMPv3 security.

sections.title: What the FTN MIB Describes
sections.content:
At the ingress of an MPLS network, packets entering the MPLS domain are assigned to a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC). Packets in an FEC are tied to a Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE), that is, an MPLS label, through the FEC-to-NHLFE (FTN) mapping from RFC 3031. This defines how ingress LSRs impose labels and how egress LSRs remove the MPLS shim header.

RFC 3814 defines the managed objects for specifying these mappings and their actions. The RFC notes that the FIB could do some of this by mapping all packets for a prefix to an LSP, but that this is coarse. It borrows the idea of match rules plus actions from security filters, access filters and RSVP flow identification. In MPLS the action is to redirect packets to either an MPLS LSP or an MPLS Traffic Engineered (TE) tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Edge routers decide which truck each parcel goes on. This document is a standard form for writing those decisions down.

sections.title: SNMP and the Management Framework
sections.content:
The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework. Managed objects live in a Management Information Base (MIB) and are normally accessed using SNMP. Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information, and this module is compliant with SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).

The module resides on any LSR that does the FEC-to-NHLFE mapping in order to bring traffic into the MPLS domain. The IANA assigned it mplsStdMIB 8, as the MPLS-FTN-STD-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the standard phone line managers use to read and change settings on network boxes. The MIB is the list of settings you are allowed to ask about.

sections.title: The Three Tables
sections.content:
The module has three tables.

  • mplsFTNTable is the rule base. Each row is an FTN entry with a match rule and an action.
  • mplsFTNMapTable applies those rules to specific interfaces.
  • mplsFTNPerfTable gives performance counters for each entry that is active on an interface, per interface.

A rule matches on a 6-tuple: source address range, destination address range, source port range, destination port range, the IPv4 protocol field or IPv6 next-header field, and the DiffServ Code Point (DSCP). The mplsFTNMask object is a bit map (sourceAddr, destAddr, sourcePort, destPort, protocol, dscp) saying which fields count. A field whose bit is zero MUST be ignored when comparing.

The action is a redirect, with a pointer either to an mplsXCEntry in the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB (RFC 3813) for a non-TE LSP, or to an mplsTunnelEntry in the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB (RFC 3812) when the NHLFE starts a TE tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: One list holds the sorting rules. A second list says which door each rule applies to. A third keeps count of parcels that matched.

sections.title: Address Ranges and the Linked-List Index
sections.content:
Rules use address ranges instead of CIDR prefixes. Some ranges need many prefixes: the range 192.0.2.0 to 192.0.2.62 needs 6 CIDR prefixes, and a rule with such a source range and a similar destination range would need 36 rows, against a single row with ranges. Every CIDR prefix can be written as a range, and an implementation may translate ranges internally.

Packets arriving on an interface are compared against FTN entries in the order they were applied. To let a manager insert an entry with a single SET and no reindexing, mplsFTNMapTable behaves like a linked list. Each row has mplsFTNMapPrevIndex, a pointer to the previous entry on that interface, and the agent adjusts it automatically after an insertion or deletion.

A manager can walk the list in order with GETNEXT operations on mplsFTNMapRowStatus. The number of retrieval operations equals the number of applied entries. A 'next' pointer would not let a manager find the first entry on an interface with a single retrieval.

Because an application can be disturbed by a concurrent change, it can read mplsFTNMapTableLastChanged before a traversal and include it in each GETNEXT to check that nothing changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for each door are kept like a chain of people holding hands, so a new rule can slip in between two people without everyone else moving.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through rules on interface ifIndex = 1. Rule 1 redirects packets with source IPv4 address 192.0.2.63 to an LSP with outgoing ifIndex 50 and label 150. Rule 2 redirects packets with destination addresses from 192.0.2.32 to 192.0.2.96 to tunnel 4. Rule 2 is added after Rule 1 by setting mplsFTNMapPrevIndex to 1 in its map entry.

The same FTN entry can be reused on another interface by adding one map row. Later, Rule 3 sends destination prefix 192.0.2.32/28 (the range 192.0.2.32 to 192.0.2.47) to tunnel 3. Order matters because Rule 3's range is a subset of Rule 2's, so Rule 3 is inserted after Rule 1 and before Rule 2. Only the entry right after the new one is affected, and its previous pointer adjusts automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want a special rule for a few houses on a street, you slip it in before the rule for the whole street, and nobody else needs to be renumbered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module can be used to redirect non-MPLS traffic into an MPLS cloud, so improper changes to mplsFTNTable and mplsFTNMapTable may send traffic to unintended destinations, cause denial of service, or route traffic that should enter MPLS through the IP network instead. Unauthorized reading of mplsFTNPerfTable may reveal traffic flow information.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, says that deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and makes it the operator's responsibility to give access only to legitimate principals.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever holds the sorting rule book can send parcels to the wrong place, so only trusted people should be allowed to write in it or peek at the counters.
